title: The Cockatoos Across the Strait

lines.text: Two islands two hours apart had different continents' birds.
In 1856, the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace reached Bali.
Then he sailed on to neighbouring Lombok, for about three months.
The islands look alike, with similar soils and climate.
On Bali he had seen woodpeckers. On Lombok he never saw one.
Instead there were cockatoos and brush-turkeys, Australian kinds of bird.
He wrote that 'we may pass in two hours from one great division of the earth to another'.
The sea between Java, Borneo and Asia is shallow. He reasoned they were joined to Asia not long ago.
To the east, far deeper water pointed to a long separation.
Thomas Henry Huxley later named the boundary Wallace's Line.
Some of nature's sharpest borders follow old gaps in the sea that animals could not cross.
Sulawesi, east of the line, has marsupials. Borneo, to its west, has none.
lines.say: Soo-lah-way-see, east of the line, has marsupials. Borneo, to its west, has none.

caption: Wallace sailed fifteen miles from Bali to Lombok and crossed from Asian birds to Australian ones. The border is called Wallace's Line, and it follows deep water. A true story, fact-checked. Curiouser No. 10
